strengths: An intuitive and well-motivated architecture that successfully merges Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) with Slimmable Neural Networks to provide a continuous compute-accuracy trade-off.
The proposed pre-training recipe is simple, stable, and introduces minimal training overhead compared to traditional MoE pipelines.
The introduction of test-time training (TTT) to calibrate the sharpness parameter $\gamma$ under a fixed budget is a clever and effective way to handle inference-time capacity allocation.
Extensive experiments, ablations, and visualizations (e.g., the breakdown of FLOPs, analysis of the learned $\gamma$, and out-of-domain transfer) thoroughly validate the effectiveness of the method.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to smaller-scale models (up to 1B parameters) and limited token budgets compared to modern state-of-the-art LLMs, leaving the scalability to massive LLMs unconfirmed.

Efficiency is evaluated primarily in theoretical FLOPs. Dynamic slicing of weight matrices on GPUs can introduce kernel launch overheads, memory alignment issues, and batching difficulties, which may significantly impact actual wall-clock latency.
The paper lacks a direct empirical comparison with other dynamic or adaptive computation baselines for MoE, such as adaptive top-$k$ routing or token-skipping methods.

strengths: Well-motivated integration of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and slimmable networks, unlocking an extra dimension of conditional computation (expert selection and expert width).

A simple yet effective test-time training (TTT) mechanism that optimizes a very low-dimensional mapping (the sharpness parameter γ) on a small calibration set, allowing adaptive width allocation under a specified compute budget without updating the backbone parameters.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations spanning multiple model configurations (GPT2-Small, Standard, Medium) and routing budgets, showing consistent shifts in the Pareto frontier (lower perplexity at lower MFLOPs).
Excellent presentation, clear figures, and high reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to relatively small, historical model sizes (up to 1B parameters) trained on small datasets (OpenWebText). It remains unclear how these findings scale to modern, state-of-the-art sparse MoEs (e.g., Mixtral/DeepSeek scale).

The compute savings are primarily reported in theoretical metrics (MFLOPs per token). In practice, dynamic tensor slicing at token-level or layer-level might suffer from substantial memory bandwidth and kernel launch overheads on standard GPU hardware. The paper lacks real wall-clock latency or throughput measurements to show practical speedup.

The proposed pre-training recipe requires executing the model twice per mini-batch (once at full width and once at a random width) to compute and backpropagate the joint loss. This significantly increases the training cost (up to 1.5x-2x pre-training FLOPs), which is a non-trivial overhead for large models.

strengths: The core idea of combining Mixture of Experts (MoE) with slimmable networks (MoSE) is highly intuitive and well-motivated, addressing the rigid 'all-or-nothing' execution of activated experts in standard MoE.

The paper explores multiple execution modes, including a novel Test-Time Training (TTT) formulation to calibrate the sharpness parameter $\gamma$ per layer for adaptive, budget-aware width allocation.
The paper is very well-written, featuring clear mathematical formulations, illustrative diagrams, and consistent empirical trends.
The theoretical evaluation is comprehensive, showing consistent Pareto improvements in perplexity vs. FLOPs across multiple model sizes and routing configurations.
weaknesses: The most critical weakness is the absence of wall-clock latency or throughput measurements on physical hardware (GPUs/TPUs). Dynamic, token-level matrix slicing can significantly degrade GPU Tensor Core utilization, cause memory fragmentation, and increase kernel launch overheads. Without real hardware benchmarks, the claimed 'efficiency' remains purely theoretical and may even result in slower real-world speed compared to static models.

The experimental evaluation is restricted to smaller-scale GPT-2 architectures (up to 1B parameters) trained on the OpenWebText corpus with limited token budgets. Modern MoE models utilize SwiGLU FFN layers (which involve three projections: gate, up, and down) and are trained on trillions of tokens. It is unclear how easily MoSE scales to SwiGLU or if the training stability holds at modern pre-training scales.

The proposed Test-Time Training (TTT) requires running forward and backward passes over a calibration dataset to optimize the sharpness parameter $\gamma$. The paper does not provide the concrete wall-clock time and memory overheads associated with this calibration phase, which could limit its practicality in dynamic deployment scenarios.

The paper lacks an qualitative analysis of how expert specialization interacts with the nested, slimmable structure. It would be valuable to understand if slimming an expert disproportionately hurts its specialized knowledge or if the representation remains robustly compressed.

strengths: Well-motivated and natural integration of slimmable networks with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), addressing the compute-accuracy discontinuity in standard MoEs.
Comprehensive empirical validation spanning multiple model scales (from 55M up to 2.5B parameters) and finer-grained routing configurations (e.g., E64A8, E128A8).
Clever use of a lightweight Test-Time Training (TTT) mechanism to learn the sharpness parameter, which optimally maps router confidence scores to expert execution widths.
The inclusion of continual pre-training (CPT) experiments on a 16B parameter DeepSeek model shows that the method can be practically adapted to existing strong checkpoints.
Excellent diagnostic analyses, including routing stability checks, expert utilization heatmaps, and empirical validation of latency tracking FLOP reductions.
weaknesses: Details regarding the actual hardware implementation and batched inference execution of variable-width experts are scarce. Slicing matrices dynamically at runtime for different experts within a batch (heterogeneous execution) typically suffers from massive GPU kernel launch overhead and memory alignment issues unless highly optimized custom Triton/CUDA kernels are used. It is unclear if Figure 16 represents serialized execution or fully batched throughput with custom kernels.

While FLOPs are reduced at inference time, the memory footprint remains unchanged because all parameters of the slimmable experts must reside in GPU memory. Since memory capacity is often the primary bottleneck for deploying LLMs, this limits the practical utility of the proposed method in memory-constrained environments.
The scale of from-scratch pretraining is relatively small compared to modern LLM standards (e.g., GPT2-Large on only 50B tokens), although the authors mitigate this via CPT.

strengths: Intuitive and elegant concept: Extending conditional computation in MoEs from expert selection (discrete) to expert capacity (continuous) via slimmable networks is a natural, highly promising direction that addresses a key design limitation of standard MoEs.

Lightweight adaptation mechanism (TTT): The proposed test-time training of the sharpness parameter $\gamma$ provides a remarkably simple, robust, and low-overhead way to dynamically adapt the compute budget at inference time without retraining the model's main parameters.

Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: The authors evaluate the method across multiple scales (up to 2.5B GPT-style models from scratch and a 16B DeepSeek model via continual pre-training) and confirm consistent Pareto frontier improvements.

Thorough diagnostics: The inclusion of detailed routing diagnostics (e.g., coefficient of variation of loads, normalized entropy, and JS divergence) confirms that the multi-width objective does not destabilize the router or cause expert collapse.
weaknesses: Challenges with batched inference and dynamic shapes: A major challenge of slimmable architectures in practice is execution efficiency during batched inference (batch size > 1). If different tokens in a batch route to experts with different active widths, it introduces irregular execution shapes. Without specialized kernel support or grouping, compilers often pad to the maximum width in the batch, which can nullify the latency/throughput benefits of slimmed experts. The manuscript would be significantly stronger if it addressed batched serving performance.

Missing implementation details for runtime benchmarks: While the paper includes runtime benchmarks (latency and throughput vs. FLOPs in Figure 16), it lacks details on the batch size, hardware implementation specifics, and whether any custom GPU kernels were used to handle the slicing of active expert layers at runtime.

strengths: Highly intuitive and conceptually elegant integration of slimmable networks (weight slicing) with sparsely gated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to enable dual-axis conditional computation (routing and expert capacity).
The proposed lightweight test-time training (TTT) mechanism to calibrate the routing-to-width mapping parameter (γ) is a clever and practical way to handle arbitrary compute budgets at runtime.
Strong and diverse empirical evaluation spanning multiple model sizes (up to 2.5B from scratch) and a 16B DeepSeek-V2-Lite model adapted via continual pre-training (CPT).

Extensive and thorough analyses in the appendix, including runtime diagnostics, routing stability checks, and visualization of the learned calibration parameters, showing that the multi-width objective does not destabilize the routing behavior.
weaknesses: Although FLOPs are heavily reduced, dynamic slicing of matrix dimensions per expert/token can introduce challenges for memory alignment and kernel execution on modern parallel hardware (GPUs/TPUs). The paper would benefit from a more detailed discussion or benchmarks of actual batch-level wall-clock speedups under realistic deployment frameworks (such as vLLM).

The baseline comparisons are mostly restricted to standard MoE and uniform-width execution. Comparing or discussing against other dynamic-compute MoE baselines (such as dynamic-k routing, where different tokens route to a variable number of experts) would help contextualize the performance gains.
